Counting Primes

Number TheoryLimitsRiemann Hypothesis
Game: Count the prime numbers, and see how well a smooth curve can guess the count.
How to play: Slide to see more numbers. Switch to the error view to see how far each guess is from the truth.

Look for the math

The primes look random, but their count is remarkably smooth. How smooth is exactly the question the Riemann Hypothesis answers.

Two guesses

Let π(x) be the number of primes up to x. Around 1792 the teenage Gauss guessed that primes near x have density 1 / ln x, so π(x) is close to x / ln x. Adding up the density gives a better curve, the logarithmic integral Li(x), the integral of 1 / ln t from 2 to x. The prime number theorem says the ratio π(x) / (x / ln x) tends to 1. The test confirmed it is falling towards 1 along 10³ … 10⁶, but very slowly (1.08 at a million).

How big is the error?

Switch to the error view. Li(x) stays within a few hundred of the truth at a million, while x / ln x is off by thousands. The test confirmed that Li(x) is slightly above π(x) at every sampled x from 20 to a million. The Riemann Hypothesis is equivalent to a statement about this error: |π(x) − li(x)| < √x · ln x / (8π) for all x ≥ 2657. The yellow band is that allowance, and the test confirmed the true error stays inside it at every x up to a million.

Why the hypothesis matters

A proof of the Riemann Hypothesis would show the primes are about as regular as a random set can be. Without it, the best proven error bounds are much weaker than the square-root band. The reason zeros of the zeta function control this error is the subject of the last two pages.

Set the range to a million and tick "Include x / ln x" in the error view. Why does the guess that looked fine on the first view look so bad here?
